style.vernacular: Hilly former colonial coal-mining capital on the Udi escarpment. The Government Reserved Area keeps Georgian-style colonial houses on narrow winding roads; the rest of the city is 1-3 storey cream, white and ochre painted-render houses and shops with rust-red or grey corrugated and long-span metal roofs, with 5-10 storey bank and office blocks along Okpara Avenue and bare red laterite earth verges under mango, neem and palm trees.
style.ornament: Colonial-Georgian veranda posts and hip roofs in the Government Reserved Area; modern breeze-block screens and concrete sun-breakers on public buildings; carved-wood gates and painted wall murals on Igbo compounds; church and bank signage as blank coloured boards.

style.vernacular: Dense lagoon-side metropolis: concrete-block compounds and walk-up flats of 1-4 storeys, plastered and painted in faded pastels, under rusty or coloured corrugated-iron roofs; Afro-Brazilian stucco buildings with arched windows on the Island; glass-and-concrete towers on Victoria Island; high perimeter walls with razor wire, generator sheds and water tanks.
style.ornament: Afro-Brazilian stucco: arched windows, decorative parapets, balustraded verandahs; Yoruba carved door and veranda posts on older houses; concrete breeze-block screens and sun-shading fins on modern blocks; hand-painted shop signs and murals; generator and water-tank clutter.

sources.what: Afro-Brazilian stucco/arched houses, colonial verandahs, imported cement and corrugated iron, postmodern/concrete sun-shading, 1960s+ skyscrapers
search-result summary: most Lagos houses are concrete block; Lagos household survey 2005-06 records corrugated iron as most common roofing (~78%)
